children: Tom Barkin, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, said not much had changed between the Federal Open Market Committee's meetings in July and September. "But that is precisely why it was appropriate for the
t our stance," he said in a speech in Baltimore on Tuesday.

Unemployment has remained low, economic growth has continued, and inflation has remained above the Fed's 2% goal. "With inflation more than a percentage point above target, that’s a problem," Barkin said.

For months, some economists have been arguing that recent supply shocks will fade and inflation will follow. "One problem with that argument, of course, is that the 'passing' shocks aren’t proving to be short-lived, or one-off events," he said. "New tariffs are still cropping up. The conflict in the Middle East is ongoing. And the AI build-out continues to stress those supply chains."

Those stressors may pass in time, but as inflation persists, so does the risk that current elevated inflation will affect future inflation. In his conversations with business contacts, Barkin said he's hearing that there's less resistance to price increases than there was before the pandemic. He's seeing more firms taking the chance of raising prices.
"The net of all this is more inflationary pressure. And that’s why we needed to act," he said.

Looking ahead, Barkin points to two paths. He said he's open to the possibility that inflation will come down quickly on its own. "Consumers could start to reach their limit," he noted. "The investment boom could slow. Markets could correct. Employment could falter, making the labor market the problem child."

But with the temporary shocks dragging on, inflation could prove more stubborn. "New cost pressures could develop," Barkin said. "Firming demand conditions could flow through to prices, as could the impact of today’s inflation." That scenario is likely to require further rate hikes.

"As I had to learn with my own teenagers, you can never be too confident that you know what’s going on with them," he said, comparing the Fed's dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability with raising children. "You have to ask a lot of questions, pay close attention to every signal, and stay committed to keeping them on the right path," he concluded.

Traders are leaning toward a rate hike at the October meeting with a 55.4% probability of another 25-basis-point rate hike at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Trades on the prediction market platform Kalshi, meanwhile, put the probability at 51%.

title: The time was right to hike as inflation remains a 'problem child,' Richmond Fed's Barkin says
